stories: TNC's Mount Hamilton Wilderness campaign: Initially, silicon Valley groups wanted to protect open spaces but didn't know where to start. When TNC named the brown hills 'Mount Hamilton Wilderness' (after its highest peak with a local observatory), local interest increased. The Packard Foundation (created by a Hewlett-Packard founder) provided a large grant. Other environmental groups started campaigning to preserve the area. Sweeney admits the brown hills aren't visually 'sexy'—covered in brown grass with oak trees—but TNC pursued it 'because it's an ecologically important part of creation.' Now other groups reference the Mount Hamilton Wilderness in their documents.
summary: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) discovered that 40% of California needed environmental protection, but couldn't afford to buy all the land. By shifting from a 'bucks and acres' strategy to a landscape-based approach, TNC made its mission more concrete and tangible. Instead of discussing 2 million acres, TNC set a goal to preserve 50 landscapes (25 as immediate priority) over ten years. The Mount Hamilton Wilderness example shows how naming and defining an area transforms abstract land conservation into a tangible 'eco-celebrity' that engages donors and policymakers.
